cues.text: The World Food Program and the United Nations Food and Agriculture Agency reported that rising global food and fuel prices piled onto those local problems.
Some staple foods reached prices that many poor households couldn't afford.
When the local harvest is poor, imported grain can help make up the difference.
In Somalia that year, it was getting more expensive right when people needed it most.
Then there was a bill that could get more expensive even if you bought nothing new.
If you were carrying a credit card balance, you might open your statement one month and find a higher interest charge.
It would be easy to put that increase in the same category as the gas bill.
The dates tell a different story.
In January, before the full -scale invasion, US consumer prices were already up 7 .5 % from a year earlier.
The Federal Reserve had signaled that it expected to raise rates soon.
When it did raise them in March, it pointed to price pressure stemming from the pandemic and described the invasion as likely to add to inflation in the near term.
The war added pressure to a problem the Fed was already preparing to act on.
What can higher rates do about prices?
If financing the next car gets more expensive, some buyers delay replacing the one they have.
If fewer people buy, sellers face less pressure from demand.
That's where the Fed has leverage.
Interest rates have much less to say about whether a ship can load grain at a Ukrainian port.
And which borrowing bill changes depends on what you signed.
A homeowner's principle and interest on an existing fixed -rate mortgage are set by the loan.
A credit card rate tied to a benchmark can go up when that benchmark rises, so a balance carried over from last month can cost more this month.
By the end of 2022, US regular gasoline averaged $3 .09 a gallon below where it had started the year.
Refineries were making more gasoline in the second half of the year, and Americans were using less.
At the grocery store, food prices were still higher than they had been a year earlier.
The station could buy its next delivery for less, as gasoline became easier to come by.
For the bakery, cheaper wheat helped only if it brought down the price of flour.
The cost of getting the next batch of bread to the store could still be high.
On that same drive home, you could spend less than you'd set aside for gas.
A few minutes later, a week's groceries could eat up the difference.
